beats.trigger: ## Getting Going
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: With the right guardrails, you create output that's genuinely yours, not generic.
beats.got: Claim with no number attached; 'genuinely yours' is not something I can put in a board paper.

beats.trigger: Connect your calendar (M365 / Google Workspace / screenshot fallback) and save a 5-line summary of this week's meetings.
beats.got: Homework that needs my calendar connected to an AI tool, which IT has not approved.

beats.trigger: **Package** the guardrails as reusable rules
beats.got: Four verbs, no outcome. Nothing about cost or payback.

beats.trigger: **The question, to you:** where did LLM output on your own work come out generic, and what made it feel like yours?
beats.got: I have barely used it, so I have no answer. It also asks what it 'felt like', which I don't care for.

beats.trigger: The same question. Two answers. What makes the difference?
beats.got: A teaser. Fine, short.

beats.trigger: The first exchange became context.
beats.got: The earlier questions change the dinner answer, so the tool is steered by what came before. That is simple and checkable.

beats.trigger: The LLM reads the whole conversation every time and generates the next response from all of it.
beats.got: It rereads everything each time. So inputs drive outputs, which I can understand.

beats.trigger: You told the LLM who you are.
beats.got: Telling it a role changes the answer. A cardiologist example is clear enough.

beats.trigger: Tools, goals, checks, boundaries, and loops come later and depend on it.
beats.got: A list of future words with no content yet.

beats.trigger: You write it once, and it shapes every answer.
beats.got: A file the agent reads each session. Write once, reuse. That sounds like a cost saver, if it works.

beats.trigger: Change the context, watch the agent's output shift, then package what you learned for the next session.
beats.got: 45 minutes on something I have not seen a business reason for yet.

beats.trigger: **Open your own LinkedIn profile in your browser.**
beats.got: I am building a personal website from my LinkedIn. I am a CFO, not a brand. Nothing about my finance work.

beats.trigger: A colleague who lands on it should think *"this is the person I want to work with more, on the things they're great at,"*
beats.got: Nothing. This is a vanity site and I would never publish it.

beats.trigger: The LLM already knows StoryBrand, so you don't reproduce the questions.
beats.got: You can name a known framework and ask the agent to run it. The idea is useful, the example is not for me.

beats.trigger: Answer each in your own words, briefly; don't polish.
beats.got: The agent questions me through five beats about myself. I'd rather do this with my variance report.

beats.trigger: Your strengths shape how the whole site sounds.
beats.got: Nothing new. List strengths, regenerate.

beats.trigger: Most people can list what drives them mad at work in thirty seconds, but stall for five minutes on what they're great at.
beats.got: True of me. Listing what I dislike is easier. It is mildly amusing.

beats.trigger: Vague input drifts back to the statistical-default you.
beats.got: Specific input gives specific output, vague gives average. That applies to my own prompts as well.

beats.trigger: The agent is reading its own work where it wrote it, and LLMs go easy on their own output.
beats.got: It admits the tool grades its own work too kindly. A risk named before I had to ask it.

beats.trigger: *"Make it look like Stripe's design language"*
beats.got: Colours and fonts. I'm checking my inbox.

beats.trigger: so a fresh agent can repeat it on someone else's bio without you re-explaining.
beats.got: The agent writes down the method as a rules file, so the next person does not start from zero. That is reuse, the first time I see value.

beats.trigger: The more specific the context, the more the output is yours.
beats.got: Specific context gives specific output. I agree, but I knew it from the dinner example.

beats.trigger: The LLM didn't get better between Phase 1 and Phase 6. You got better at feeding it the context that produces YOUR output.
beats.got: The gain came from my inputs, not from a better model. It lists compliance reviews and competitor analysis, but with no figures.

beats.trigger: ## Iterate and Learn
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The durable result is what you can now package: what context the agent needs, what generic looks like, what a stronger pass does differently, and which rule should survive into the next session.
beats.got: The lasting output is the rules, not the site.

beats.trigger: Grading its own work is another chance to be helpful: the self-report is the same kind of output as the thing reported on.
beats.got: Do not let it audit itself. It is like letting the auditee sign off the audit.

beats.trigger: Read what comes back as a claim about the work, not a verdict on it.
beats.got: Treat the output as a claim to verify. That is how I treat everything already.

beats.trigger: Only you could catch a wrong line about you, which is why your own profile is the place to start.
beats.got: The human with the domain knowledge is the check. Reasonable.

beats.trigger: Reading a McKinsey report on the agentic enterprise gives you opinions about a future.
beats.got: Honest that nobody knows, but it is a 'run the experiment' pitch with no budget or payback.

beats.trigger: Expect the generation rules to change a lot. The first pass is rarely right.
beats.got: The first version is wrong and gets fixed in a second pass. Honest, and it is just normal review.

beats.trigger: Repeat on every rules file: do the work → capture → reflect → sharpen.
beats.got: Each review round improves the file. Fine, but not new to me.

beats.trigger: Your gut on what is uniquely you carries more weight than the agent's.
beats.got: Use a second reader that has not seen the work. An independent check, which is good.

beats.trigger: Output got specific because the context did.
beats.got: Three lines, fair. Still no cost.

beats.trigger: Bring a live challenge and working access to Confluence and OneDrive.
beats.got: I would have to ask IT for access to company documents, which will not be quick.

beats.trigger: Karpathy's LLM Wiki post; Lindenberg's memory-architecture piece, optional.
beats.got: More reading and I'm not doing it.

beats.trigger: Module 2 works on real history: meetings, notes, decisions, half-written documents.
beats.got: Module 2 uses real work material, not my LinkedIn. That is better.

beats.trigger: If stuck, scan your next two weeks of calendar; the biggest unresolved item is usually your challenge.
beats.got: Start from a real open problem. Mine is month-end variance or forecasting. I can name that.

beats.trigger: If a connector needs admin approval, tell the training coordinator and keep going.
beats.got: Connecting the tool to company files needs approval. GDPR and finance data are where IT will say no, and the module doesn't raise it.

beats.trigger: Before it writes anything, ask it for a plan and approve or revise it first.
beats.got: Approve the plan before the agent acts. That is a control I would require on anything touching finance files.

beats.trigger: If a line is blank, name a fallback; do not fill it with a plausible answer.
beats.got: Write down three things and admit what is missing instead of guessing. I agree with that.

beats.trigger: a useful system is a living pile of text the agent can read, maintain, and improve.
beats.got: More homework from a blog post.

beats.trigger: The output now travels with a file the agent re-reads next time.
beats.got: The rules file carries over to the next session.

take_homes: What I put in decides what comes out, so vague input gives average output.
Don't let the agent grade its own work. Check it with my own knowledge or a second, independent reader.
Ask for a plan and approve it before the agent writes to files, and keep the lessons in a rules file the next session reads.

monday.move: Ask my controller to try the month-end variance commentary with an agent, with a plan approved first and the output checked by her against the ledger.
monday.when: Next month-end close, not this week
monday.stop_condition: If it takes longer than writing the commentary by hand, or any figure doesn't tie to the ledger, we stop.
monday.blocker: IT has not approved the tool for finance data, and nobody has said what it costs per month.

misconception.why: The rules file that carries over to the next session made me see that some of the value is what we write down and keep, not just the licence. But nothing in the day mentioned cost, so I still think of it as a purchase until someone shows me the numbers.

one_line: Two good ideas, that input decides output and that the agent shouldn't grade itself, buried in 45 minutes of building a website about me with no mention of cost or payback.
